title: What is EBS, what are the volume types (gp3/gp2 general-purpose SSD, io1/io2 provisioned IOPS, st1/sc1 HDD), and why is gp3 usually preferred over gp2 (decoupled IOPS/throughput, cheaper)?
shortTitle: EBS, Volume Types, and Why gp3 Over gp2

s1_definition.profdef: Amazon Elastic Block Store (EBS) provides durable, network-attached block storage volumes for EC2 instances, behaving like a virtual hard disk that persists independently of the instance's life. EBS offers several volume types: gp2 and gp3 are general-purpose SSDs, io1 and io2 are provisioned-IOPS SSDs for the highest, most consistent performance, and st1 (throughput-optimized) and sc1 (cold) are HDDs for large sequential workloads at low cost. gp3 is usually preferred over gp2 because it lets you set IOPS and throughput independently of size and is cheaper per gigabyte, whereas gp2's performance is tied to its size.
s1_definition.analogy: Think of an EC2 server as a desk where a clerk at National Bank of India works, and EBS as the filing cabinet bolted next to the desk. The cabinet holds all the clerk's documents, and even if the clerk goes home (the instance stops), the cabinet and its documents stay. gp2 is an older cabinet where the speed of pulling out files depends on how big the cabinet is — a small cabinet is slow. gp3 is a newer cabinet where you can dial the speed up or down separately from the size, and it costs less, so you pay only for the speed you actually need.
s1_definition.oneliner: EBS is a persistent virtual disk for EC2, and gp3 beats gp2 because you tune IOPS and throughput separately from size and pay less.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Amazon Elastic Block Store (EBS) provides durable, network-attached block storage volumes for EC2 instances, behaving like a virtual hard disk that persists independently of the instance's life. EBS offers several volume types: gp2 and gp3 are general-purpose SSDs, io1 and io2 are provisioned-IOPS SSDs for the highest, most consistent performance, and st1 (throughput-optimized) and sc1 (cold) are HDDs for large sequential workloads at low cost. gp3 is usually preferred over gp2 because it lets you set IOPS and throughput independently of size and is cheaper per gigabyte, whereas gp2's performance is tied to its size.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Think of an EC2 server as a desk where a clerk at National Bank of India works, and EBS as the filing cabinet bolted next to the desk. The cabinet holds all the clerk's documents, and even if the clerk goes home (the instance stops), the cabinet and its documents stay. gp2 is an older cabinet where the speed of pulling out files depends on how big the cabinet is — a small cabinet is slow. gp3 is a newer cabinet where you can dial the speed up or down separately from the size, and it costs less, so you pay only for the speed you actually need.

**One line to remember:** EBS is a persistent virtual disk for EC2, and gp3 beats gp2 because you tune IOPS and throughput separately from size and pay less.

sections.s2_technical:
EBS volumes are network-attached, which means the storage lives separately from the physical host and is replicated within an Availability Zone for durability. Because it is a block device, the operating system formats it with a filesystem and uses it like a local disk. The key property is persistence: if an instance is stopped or even terminated (when the volume is not set to delete on termination), the EBS volume and its data survive and can be re-attached to another instance.

The general-purpose SSD types, gp2 and gp3, suit most workloads such as boot volumes and database files for a medium banking service. With gp2, performance is tied to volume size: you get three IOPS per gigabyte, so a small volume is slow and you must over-provision size just to get speed. With gp3, you get a baseline of 3000 IOPS and 125 megabytes per second of throughput regardless of size, and you can pay to increase IOPS up to 16000 and throughput up to 1000 megabytes per second independently, decoupled from capacity.

```java
// Illustrating the gp2-vs-gp3 difference as a simple calculation
int sizeGiB = 100;
int gp2Iops = sizeGiB * 3;           // gp2: locked to 3 IOPS per GiB = 300 IOPS
int gp3BaselineIops = 3000;          // gp3: 3000 baseline regardless of size
int gp3ProvisionedIops = 6000;       // gp3: can raise independently of size
```

The provisioned-IOPS SSD types, io1 and io2, are for workloads that need the highest and most predictable performance, such as a large transactional database for the core banking ledger. io2 improves on io1 with higher durability and a better IOPS-to-size ratio, and io2 Block Express reaches hundreds of thousands of IOPS. You pay a premium, so you use these only where consistent low-latency performance is critical.

The HDD types, st1 and sc1, are magnetic and optimized for large, sequential throughput rather than small random reads. st1 suits big streaming workloads like log processing or data warehousing, and sc1 is the cheapest, for cold data you rarely touch. They cannot be boot volumes.

A senior nuance: migrating a volume from gp2 to gp3 is done live with Elastic Volumes and typically cuts cost by around twenty percent while giving a guaranteed 3000 IOPS baseline, which for a small boot volume is often faster than gp2's size-derived IOPS. The main reason to stay on provisioned IOPS rather than gp3 is when you need more than 16000 IOPS or sub-millisecond consistency, which gp3 cannot guarantee.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — National Bank of India runs a reporting service on EC2 with a 100 gigabyte data volume. On gp2 that volume gives only 300 IOPS because gp2 ties speed to size, and the reports are slow at month end. The team's instinct is to grow the volume to 1000 gigabytes just to get more IOPS, wasting money on space they do not need. This is exactly what gp3 solves: it gives a 3000 IOPS baseline on the same 100 gigabytes and lets you raise IOPS without buying extra space.

Problem 2 — The core ledger database needs guaranteed, consistent high IOPS no matter what. For this one workload gp3's ceiling is not enough and consistency must be rock solid. This is exactly what io2 provisioned IOPS solves.

We will write a small volume-recommendation engine. `EbsVolume` models a volume with a type, size, and provisioned IOPS. `VolumeAdvisor` computes the effective IOPS for gp2 (size times three) versus gp3 (baseline or provisioned) and recommends the cheaper option that meets a required IOPS. The demo compares the 100 gigabyte reporting volume on gp2 and gp3, and flags the ledger for io2.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: a 100 gigabyte reporting volume evaluated first as gp2 then as gp3 with 6000 provisioned IOPS, a required IOPS of 3000, and a separate core-ledger requirement of 50000 IOPS with strict consistency.

Step 1. The advisor computes the effective IOPS for the gp2 reporting volume. Because gp2 gives three IOPS per gigabyte, a 100 gigabyte volume yields only 300 IOPS. The data here is the volume size driving the speed.

Step 2. The advisor compares 300 IOPS against the required 3000 and logs a warning: gp2 falls far short, and the only gp2 remedy is to grow the volume to 1000 gigabytes, paying for 900 gigabytes of unused space purely to buy speed.

Step 3. The advisor computes the effective IOPS for the gp3 reporting volume. gp3 gives a 3000 IOPS baseline and here is provisioned to 6000, all on the same 100 gigabytes, because gp3 decouples IOPS from size. The size stayed at 100 gigabytes but the speed went up.

Step 4. The advisor makes a recommendation for the reporting workload. Since 3000 IOPS is needed and there is no strict-consistency requirement, it recommends gp3, which meets the need and costs about twenty percent less than gp2.

Step 5. The advisor evaluates the core ledger, which needs 50000 IOPS and strict consistency. Because that exceeds gp3's 16000 ceiling and demands consistency, it recommends io2 provisioned IOPS.

Step 6. The final output logs the gp2 shortfall, the gp3 improvement, and the two recommendations.

```
2026-10-29 01:55:00 [INFO] Reporting on gp2 (100 GiB): effective IOPS = 300
2026-10-29 01:55:00 [WARNING] gp2 gives only 300 IOPS but we need 3000 — would need to over-provision size
2026-10-29 01:55:00 [INFO] Reporting on gp3 (100 GiB): effective IOPS = 6000 (decoupled from size, ~20% cheaper)
2026-10-29 01:55:00 [INFO] Recommendation for reporting: gp3 (3000 IOPS baseline, raise IOPS/throughput independently, cheaper than gp2)
2026-10-29 01:55:00 [INFO] Recommendation for core ledger (needs consistency): io2 (provisioned IOPS, highest + consistent performance)
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  Required IOPS + consistency need
    │
    ▼
  ┌──────────────────────────────┐
  │        VolumeAdvisor         │
  │  effectiveIops(volume)       │
  └───────┬──────────────────────┘
          │
  ┌───────┴─────────────────────────────────┐
  │ gp2: IOPS = size × 3  (tied to size)     │ 100 GiB → 300 IOPS
  │ gp3: max(3000, provisioned) (decoupled)  │ 100 GiB → 6000 IOPS
  │ io2: provisioned (consistent, premium)   │ up to 256K IOPS
  └───────┬─────────────────────────────────┘
          ▼
  recommend(requiredIops, needsConsistency)
    ├─ consistency OR >16000 IOPS → io2
    └─ otherwise                   → gp3 (cheaper than gp2)

  Volume persists independent of EC2:
    [EC2 stop] → EBS volume + data SURVIVE → re-attach to new EC2
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Amazon Elastic Block Store, or EBS, is durable network-attached block storage for EC2 instances. It behaves like a virtual hard disk that the operating system formats and uses like a local drive, but it is replicated within an Availability Zone for durability and, crucially, it persists independently of the instance, so if I stop or terminate the instance the volume and its data survive and can be re-attached elsewhere.

There are four families. The general-purpose SSDs, gp2 and gp3, cover most workloads like boot volumes and medium databases. The provisioned-IOPS SSDs, io1 and io2, are for the highest and most consistent performance, such as a large core-banking ledger. The HDDs, st1 and sc1, are magnetic and tuned for large sequential throughput at low cost, for things like log processing and cold data, and they cannot be boot volumes.

The reason I almost always prefer gp3 over gp2 is that gp2 ties performance to size — it gives only three IOPS per gigabyte, so a small volume is slow and you end up over-provisioning capacity just to buy speed. gp3 decouples performance from size: it gives a flat 3000 IOPS and 125 megabytes per second baseline no matter the size, and I can raise IOPS and throughput independently up to 16000 IOPS and 1000 megabytes per second. On top of that gp3 is roughly twenty percent cheaper per gigabyte, and I can migrate from gp2 to gp3 live with Elastic Volumes.

At National Bank of India our reporting service ran a 100 gigabyte gp2 data volume that gave only 300 IOPS, and the team wanted to inflate it to a terabyte just to get speed. I moved it to gp3, which gave a 3000 IOPS baseline on the same 100 gigabytes and let me provision up to 6000 IOPS without buying unused space, cutting cost at the same time. The one place I kept provisioned IOPS was the core ledger database, where I used io2 because it needs more than gp3's ceiling and demands rock-solid, consistent low latency — that is the specific case where I do not use gp3.
